prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock rests on one clear physical idea, the magic wavelength, at which the lattice light shifts the two clock levels equally so that Doppler and recoil effects vanish while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. Katori proposed it and made the early strontium demonstrations. Ye's group then took the clocks to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, resolved the redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, and developed the systematics control and many-body understanding behind that number. The result is quantitative, theory and experiment agree in detail, and many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) build and compare these clocks. It is the most broadly supported ballot after the opening round, with seven of eight members ranking it, and I do not equate that with merit. I rest the case on its merits: a new observable regime (gravitational time dilation in the laboratory, bounds on varying constants and dark matter, the coming redefinition of the second), a clean two-person credit that matches the supplied names, and a step distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a measurement-technology prize. Colleagues who weigh surprise and new states of matter highly may find it incremental relative to the 2005 comb prize, and the headline fundamental physics (varying constants, dark matter, a clock-based redefinition of the second) has not yet been delivered. The credit also has soft edges: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, the Hg lattice clock, and the ion-clock community (Wineland's 2012 prize, Al+ clocks) could be argued to deserve a place. Katori and Ye are the most defensible pair, but not the only one. As an atomic physicist I am also inside this community and may favour its virtues.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement method that opens new observation, notes the 1e-18 level, redshift over millimetres and the path to redefining the second, and treats Katori and Ye as a clean two-person configuration with minor priority questions about Hg clocks and Lemonde.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and we ranked it first independently. I would qualify the priority point more than you do: the Hg lattice proposal and the SYRTE work are not trivial, and I would want the committee to confirm that the magic-wavelength concept is Katori's and not a shared origin before we settle on two names. On your second choice, atom interferometry, I agree on the science but disagree with your trio. Adding Mlynek alongside Pritchard and Kasevich is defensible for the double-slit and grating experiments, but it blurs the grating and light-pulse approaches, and Chu's absence remains an awkward fact, so I would keep this as an alternative, not the main prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window: a cubic-kilometre ice detector, a confirmed diffuse flux, and later source evidence from TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the credited leaders. He also ranks the optical lattice clock second.
responses.response: I defer to you on the astrophysics and I accept the claim that the diffuse flux is robust across several analysis channels. My concern is attribution. You rely on general knowledge of the roles, and the pioneering Baikal and AMANDA work that Ulf also flags is a real complication for how Spiering is credited. A three-name prize for a collaboration of hundreds is not sufficient on its face. The clocks, by contrast, trace to two named people. Since we agree on the lattice clock as a top-two candidate, I think the discussion should settle whether the IceCube credit question can be resolved cleanly before ranking it above B012.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first: the Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall state as a universal mechanism with protected edge channels, with Molenkamp's HgTe experiment as the measured counterpart. He concedes that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a real gap and that the 2016 prize covers part of the area.
responses.response: I agree the idea is deep and generates a field, and I take your point that the mechanism is clean. But you have named the weakness yourself. A trio without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang rewards the HgTe experiment without crediting the theory that told Molenkamp where to look, and the 2016 topological-phase prize already honoured part of this territory. I would need that credit question resolved before I would rank it above a candidate with a clear two-name attribution. I defer to you on the condensed-matter side; if you can show that the Kane-Mele theory alone is separable, that would change my view.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a predicted flat-band condition confirmed by experiment, opening correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean tunable platform, reproduced worldwide, with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero as the theory-experiment split.
responses.response: This is the kind of surprise I like, a quantitative prediction followed by an unexpected result, and I see why it ranks high for you. I am less sure it is ready. Bernhard and Eva Olsson both note that the origin of the correlated and superconducting phases is still debated, and the credit between Bistritzer and MacDonald on one side and the 2018 experimental trio on the other is not settled. I defer to you on the condensed-matter judgement, but I would put this as a strong candidate for the following years and not the one to complete now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a new regime of light-matter physics on a chip and the architecture beneath superconducting quantum processors, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf a coherent trio, and ranks the Cirac-Zoller-Blatt candidate second.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is real physics, and the attribution is cleaner than for many candidates. My hesitation is the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which already recognised the circuit-quantum-mechanics lineage, and I would not like the committee to appear to follow it with a second superconducting-circuit award immediately. I share your respect for the Cirac-Zoller-Blatt work and ranked it third, but the Wineland 2012 and Aspect-Clauser-Zeilinger 2022 prizes reduce the unclaimed ground, and Blatt's claim relative to Wineland needs care.

uncertainties: Whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration fully capture the priority, given the Hg lattice clock work and the SYRTE group and the ion-clock context.

Whether the committee regards a precision-measurement prize as sufficiently close to a discovery of nature, given the 2005 comb prize and the fact that the fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective.
Whether the IceCube credit (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) can be separated cleanly from AMANDA and Baikal, and whether three names can represent a very large collaboration.

My view of the condensed-matter candidates relies on colleagues' judgement of maturity, particularly the unresolved origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene and the uncredited theory behind HgTe.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows no connection to Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, to the lattice-clock community or to the other shortlisted candidates. My long-time collaboration with Anne L'Huillier concerns her 2023 prize and not any shortlisted ballot. I am a theoretical atomic physicist working in the same broad field as the atomic and precision-measurement candidates, but I have no specific conflict that would require recusal.
